A Missed Task, a Tired Caregiver and an Argument Are Three Different Problems

A short guide to telling care problems, caregiver overload and family disagreements apart.

Download PDF

Your father missed an appointment. Your sister, who does most of the day-to-day, sounds worn out. And the last family call ended in an argument about whose fault it is. It feels like one big problem.

It's three, and each one needs a different conversation, often with a different person. This guide explains how to tell them apart and why that comes before solving any of them. It doesn't judge your family's list or anyone on it.

One conversation can't carry everything

The Family Caregiver Alliance, in its guide to family meetings, says it will probably be difficult to cover every issue in one meeting and that a narrow focus for each meeting helps. It also says the task is not to “fix” the family. It is to have everyone on the same team, as much as possible, in caring for the person who needs it.1

So the first move is a small one: name the problem that is active now, and let the next conversation be about that. The question that keeps a call on its subject is the one about your father, which is what he wants and needs. The National Institute on Aging says the best way to know what someone needs is to ask them directly.2

  • One active problem for the next call. The others go on a list, where they won't be lost.
  • Your father's answer first, in his words, when he is able to give one.

A complaint isn't a problem yet

“Nobody is looking after him properly” is a complaint. “He missed his Tuesday appointment and no one knew until Thursday” is a problem the family can talk about. The difference between them is an example.

The Family Caregiver Alliance gives two clues that a discussion between siblings has drifted from the issue: someone generalizes (“You always do this!”), or someone criticizes the way they think another person is being, such as selfish, bossy or uncaring. Its advice is to focus just on the issue at hand.3

We'd add a habit of our own: keep what you saw apart from what you think it means. “The prescription wasn't picked up until Friday” is something you saw. “Nobody is on top of things” is a conclusion. Write down the first kind, and then ask how it touched your father's day.

  • For each complaint, look for one example with a day attached.
  • Where there isn't one, write “no example yet.” That is worth knowing too.

The person doing the most is often the last one asked

In most families, AARP's planning guide says, one person assumes the primary role because he or she lives nearby, has a close relationship, or simply is a take-charge person. The Family Caregiver Alliance adds that brothers and sisters may assume that person has everything covered, so they don't recognize the added responsibilities.43

She may not tell you. The National Institute on Aging says a primary caregiver may be hesitant to ask for help or a break, and its advice to everyone who isn't the primary caregiver is plain: ask what you can do that would be most helpful.56

It helps to see the work before anyone discusses it. The National Institute on Aging lists what caregiving can involve: personal care, household tasks, preparing food, talking to doctors and keeping track of appointments and medications, rides, and paying bills and organizing documents. Go down that list and write who does each one for your father now.7

Your sister has a great deal of company. A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving says one in every four adults is a caregiver, and that seven in ten family caregivers are employed.8

  • When someone hasn't done what they said they would, write the task and the date. Leave the adjective out.
  • If the family disagrees about a move or about bringing in more help, note who thinks what. This isn't the page where it gets settled.

Sort the list by who should hear it

Once the concerns have examples, put the ones that belong together in a group: everything about appointments, everything about who is doing what. A handful of groups is easier to talk about than a long list. For each group, say what you need, whether that is more information or help, and note who should hear it.

Some of it is the family's to talk through. Some of it isn't. If you're concerned about a person's physical or mental health, the National Institute on Aging says to suggest a visit to a health care provider. The Family Caregiver Alliance notes that many caregiving questions, such as personal care and managing medications at home, relate more to nursing than to medicine. And when a family has trouble working together, it says it often helps to invite a neutral outside person, such as a social worker.291

What this means for your family

  • One pile becomes three: the tasks that aren't getting done, what your sister needs, and what the family disagrees about.
  • Each concern gets an example, and each example gets a day.
  • Your job is to describe and to sort. It isn't to decide who was right.
  • The list doesn't have to be finished in one call. What isn't discussed this time stays on it for the next.
  • Questions about your father's health or his medications go to his doctor, the nurse or the pharmacist. What all of it adds up to is for the people who assess him.

What this guide doesn't do

It doesn't say whose account is right, whether your father is safe where he is, or what care he needs. The advice about meetings, siblings and caregivers comes from the sources below. The habit of keeping what you saw apart from what you think it means, and the sorting into three, are ours.

Ready for the next step?

You can now tell a missed task from a tired caregiver from an argument. The care interview looks at the rest of the picture: it goes through your father's situation area by area, so the problems nobody has mentioned come up alongside the ones you've sorted, and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.
